frames.title: Day 3 Agenda
frames.text:
Welcome to Day 3: Time Management, Calendar and Travel. We start with time management and productivity, move on to calendar management, then legal calendaring, and finish with travel management. Forty-four lessons in all.

By the end of today, you'll be able to prioritize and protect the executive's time, keep a calendar that actually holds under pressure, track court deadlines precisely, and plan travel end-to-end.

frames.title: Time Management & Productivity
frames.text: Section 1 of 4: Time Management and Productivity. Eighteen lessons, from prioritization frameworks to energy management and handling interruptions.

frames.title: Prioritization Frameworks
frames.text:
When everything feels important, you need a way to decide what actually gets your time.

Think of these as four different lenses. Some days there's too much on the list. Some days you know exactly what matters, but you can't concentrate. And some days the important work never happens because meetings eat it. Each tool fixes one of those problems. The four-box grid is the one you'll use most: do now, schedule, hand off and let go.

frames.title: Prioritization Frameworks
frames.text:
First, when the list is so long you don't know where to start, sort it into those four boxes. You'll find a lot of it doesn't need you at all.

Next, use short bursts of focus: about 25 minutes on one thing, then a short break. It's easier to start when you know the end is close.

Then, give the most important work its own spot on the calendar, away from email.

frames.title: Prioritization Frameworks
frames.text:
After that, every so often, ask which small share of your work is producing most of the results, and give it more of your time. Finally, don't try all four at once. Pick the one that fixes your biggest problem this week, get good at it, then add another.

Here's a situation to work through. Elias says he spends four hours a day in email and still misses important things. Using one of the four frameworks, how would you restructure his inbox day so the important work gets done?

frames.title: Quick Check
frames.text:
Quick check. Which prioritization technique focuses on the 20 percent of tasks that produce 80 percent of results? Is it the 80/20 Rule, also called the Pareto Principle, time blocking, the Eisenhower Matrix, or the Pomodoro Technique? Take a second.

It's the 80/20 Rule. Pareto's principle is about impact concentration: a small slice of effort driving most of the outcome.

frames.title: Priority Collision Handling
frames.text:
When two truly important things arrive at once, ask what actually breaks if each one waits ten minutes.

A collision isn't normal prioritizing, where one thing is obviously more urgent. Both matter, and neither can simply be postponed.

First, weigh the real cost of delay on each side. Next, where you can, do a little on both: a quick acknowledgment on one while you fully handle the other. Finally, if it's genuinely too close to call, ask. A 30-second check-in beats a wrong guess.

Take a second with this one. In the same minute, Elias asks you to get opposing counsel on the phone right now, and a major client emails that their wire transfer failed and the closing is at noon. What happens first, and why?

frames.title: Time Management
frames.text:
Knowing what matters isn't enough; you have to decide it, put it on the calendar, guard it and check it held. Most people stop after the first step, and skipping one breaks the chain.

First, decide. Before you open the calendar, ask what really deserves protected time this week. That's a judgment call, not a scheduling one. Next, block it, early, before other people's requests fill the gaps. Then, protect it, like any other meeting you've already committed to. Finally, review it. Did the protected time actually happen, or did something 'urgent' take it every time?

Here's a situation to work through. Elias says his priority this quarter is winning the Meridian arbitration. His last four weeks show only three hours spent on it. Is this a time management problem, a calendar management problem, or both? What do you change?

frames.title: Strategic Time Engineering
frames.text:
We don't just manage the executive's calendar. We design it, the way an investor decides where money goes.

Think of his time as a portfolio. Some goes to work that brings in revenue, some to long-term growth, some to legal and compliance deadlines, some to events where his reputation is on the line, and some to personal commitments that genuinely matter.

So first, before we defend a block of time, we name what it's for. If we can't, it isn't protected. It's just empty space waiting to be filled.

frames.title: Strategic Time Engineering
frames.text:
Finally, we treat the calendar as an ongoing decision, and regularly check it still matches what matters.

Think about this. Every week, Elias's Friday afternoon 'strategy time' gets taken by last-minute requests. What would investing that time on purpose look like, instead of spending it as requests arrive?

frames.title: When Time Management Fails Despite a Clean Calendar
frames.text:
No conflicts doesn't mean no problems. Picture a day that's back-to-back reactive meetings from nine to five. Technically clean. But when does the real work happen? The question isn't just 'are there any clashes?' It's 'is this week actually set up for the things that matter?'

First, check for meeting overload. Ten small meetings can crowd out the one thing that matters. Next, confirm that protected space exists for this week's most important work.

frames.title: When Time Management Fails Despite a Clean Calendar
frames.text: Then, apply the same thinking to travel weeks: the days before, during and after a trip need care too.

frames.title: When Time Management Fails Despite a Clean Calendar
frames.text:
After that, when a week goes wrong, work out why. Did we choose the wrong priority, or the right one and fail to protect it? The fix is different for each. Finally, do this check every week, not only when something falls apart.

Try this one. Elias is in London Tuesday to Thursday. Monday, the day before he flies, has seven meetings; Friday, the day after he lands, has six. What's wrong with this plan, and how would you fix the days either side of the trip?

frames.title: Energy Management vs. Time Management
frames.text:
An open slot at someone's worst hour of the day isn't really open.

Time management asks when something should happen. Energy management asks whether this person will be at their best at that moment. Most of us are sharp in the morning, strong until lunch, slump mid-afternoon, then get a second wind late in the day. That's the curve on the slide. Book a tough negotiation into the slump, and you've scheduled it for failure.

frames.title: Energy Management vs. Time Management
frames.text:
First, learn the executive's pattern. When are they sharpest, and when do they fade?

Next, save the sharp hours for work that needs a clear head, like big decisions and negotiations.

Then, check anything high-stakes against their low times before you confirm it.

frames.title: Energy Management vs. Time Management
frames.text:
After that, if it has to go in a low time, say so. Flag it as a risk rather than pretending the slot is neutral. Finally, check the pattern again now and then. Travel, new roles and life changes shift it.

Here's a scheduling puzzle. Elias is sharpest from 8 to 11 a.m. and fades after 3 p.m. This week you have a tough negotiation, a routine staff check-in, expense sign-offs and a strategy session. Where does each one go, and why?

frames.title: Time Management Requires Energy Management
frames.text:
A free slot on the calendar isn't the same as having the energy to use it.

An exhausted executive makes expensive mistakes. After a full day of mediation, an open hour at 6 p.m. has nothing left in it for a demanding call. So we avoid stacking draining meetings, protect focus time and filter out low-value requests.

First, we build recovery breaks after the genuinely demanding events on purpose, not just as gaps between meetings. Finally, we notice patterns, like a recurring meeting that always leaves him drained, and we raise it instead of silently putting up with it.

Here's a situation to work through. You support Elias at work and his family at home. His Saturday has a work call at 9, a school event at 11 and a dinner party at 7. Where would you build in recovery time, and what might you move?

frames.title: Handling Interruptions Without Losing the Day
frames.text:
One small interruption can eat your whole afternoon if you let it.

Someone leans over your desk with a 'quick question'. The question takes two minutes. The damage is the twenty minutes it takes to find your place again. In this job you can't avoid interruptions. The skill is handling them in seconds, so they stay small.

First, decide fast whether it's truly urgent, or just feels urgent because someone is standing in front of you. Next, if it can wait, write it down somewhere you'll see later. Don't try to remember it, and don't start solving it. Then, go back to exactly where you were and finish that thought. Finally, handle the things that can wait together later, in one go.

Try the four moves on this one. You're proofreading a court filing due at 4 p.m. At 3:15, a partner asks you to 'quickly' reformat a slide deck for tomorrow. What do you say, and what do you do with the request?

frames.title: Mid-Stage Task Injections
frames.text:
Before you switch to a new request, leave yourself a clear marker of where you stopped.

A task injection is a new, unrelated request landing while you're halfway through something else. Unlike a collision, the first task can usually continue. The danger is coming back and not remembering exactly where you were. That's where mistakes creep in.

First, decide: does the new request need action now, or can it wait for a safe stopping point? Next, before you switch, leave a marker: a note, a highlighted line or a saved draft. Finally, if the new task takes over completely, tell whoever is waiting on the first one.

Here's one to think about. You were interrupted while updating a client's contact details and forgot to finish. The new number never made it into the system. What habit fixes this?

frames.title: The Two-Minute Rule
frames.text:
If it takes less time to do than to write down, just do it.

Writing a tiny task down, remembering it, finding it later and coming back to it takes more effort than simply doing it. Quick things get done immediately; bigger things get scheduled properly.

frames.title: The Two-Minute Rule
frames.text:
First, be honest about the estimate. Will it really take under two minutes, or are you hoping it will?

Next, if it really is that quick, do it now.

frames.title: The Two-Minute Rule
frames.text: Then, if it starts growing once you begin, stop and give it a proper slot on the calendar.

frames.title: The Two-Minute Rule
frames.text:
After that, keep applying the rule all day, not just when you remember. Finally, look for tiny tasks that have sat on your list for days. That's the sign the habit has slipped.

Pause the video and sort these. Confirm a lunch booking, reply 'received' to a court notice, reformat a 20-page exhibit list, forward an invoice to billing and update a phone number. Which ones pass the two-minute rule?

frames.title: Batch Processing Similar Tasks
frames.text:
Your brain works faster when it does the same kind of task several times in a row.

You wouldn't chop one onion, wash the board, then come back later for the next onion. Every jump from a call to an email to a spreadsheet makes your brain warm up again. Batching means all your calls together, then all your replies, so you warm up once for each.

frames.title: Batch Processing Similar Tasks
frames.text:
First, spot the things that come up again and again: calls, replies, data entry.

Next, give each type its own block of time.

Then, let non-urgent things wait a little so they can join their batch.

frames.title: Batch Processing Similar Tasks
frames.text:
After that, if something truly urgent arrives, break the batch. Batching is a tool, not a rule. Finally, revisit your batches when your workload changes.

Here's a quick test. You batch your scheduling emails for 3 p.m. At 10 a.m., a client needs to move today's 1 p.m. meeting. Does it wait for the batch? What rule helps you decide?

frames.title: The Cost of Context-Switching
frames.text:
It takes most people over twenty minutes to get fully back into deep work after a real interruption.

And it isn't only other people's interruptions. The switches we choose cost us too. Jumping from a filing to an email to a travel booking feels productive, because we're busy all the time. But every jump means warming up again from cold, and those minutes quietly add up.

frames.title: The Cost of Context-Switching
frames.text:
First, notice when you're the one doing the jumping.

Next, use batching and focus blocks so you pay that warm-up cost fewer times a day.

Then, don't try to do two genuinely different tasks at once. It feels efficient and is almost always slower.

frames.title: The Cost of Context-Switching
frames.text:
After that, when you do switch, close off the first task properly before starting the next. Finally, try counting your switches for one day. Almost everyone is surprised.

Here's a situation to work through. A colleague says she's great at multitasking: she drafts emails during video calls and books travel while on hold. Her work has had three errors this week. How would you talk her through what's happening?

frames.title: Dual-Role Context Switching
frames.text:
When you switch between business and personal work, switch your tone on purpose, or the wrong one will slip through.

In a combined EA and PA role, you might write a formal client email and answer a family text two minutes later. Switch too fast, and a stiff tone lands in the family message, or a casual one lands with a client.

First, name which world it belongs to: business or personal. Next, finish one fully before you open the other. Finally, keep separate task lists for business and personal, even though you manage both.

Here's what that looks like. You text Sarah: 'Per our discussion, please find below the options for Saturday.' She replies, 'Are you OK? You sound like a lawyer.' What slipped, and how do you avoid it?

frames.title: Weekly Planning Rituals
frames.text:
Fifteen minutes of planning once a week saves you from rebuilding your priorities every Monday morning.

Daily planning is good for today. But some things need several days of preparation, and you only see them if you look at the whole week at once.

First, pick a fixed time each week and protect it like any meeting.

frames.title: Weekly Planning Rituals
frames.text: Then, look back at what didn't get done last week, and decide on purpose whether it still matters or can be dropped.

frames.title: Weekly Planning Rituals
frames.text:
After that, if something needs prep several days ahead, block that prep time now. Finally, defend the session. If it keeps getting bumped, it isn't a ritual anymore.

Pause the video and plan backwards. It's Friday afternoon. Next Thursday, Elias has a mediation that needs a binder, two witness calls and a travel booking. What goes on the calendar today, and for which days?

frames.title: Saying No Without Damaging Relationships
frames.text:
A quick, honest no with an alternative protects a relationship far better than a yes you can't keep.

We often say yes because no feels uncomfortable. But what damages trust is silence, a flat no with no reason, or a yes that quietly never gets done.

frames.title: Saying No Without Damaging Relationships
frames.text:
First, answer quickly. A fast no is kinder than silence.

Next, give the real reason, specifically, so it sounds like an answer, not a brush-off.

Then, offer something: a different time, a different person or part of what they asked for.

frames.title: Saying No Without Damaging Relationships
frames.text:
Finally, if you're genuinely full, say so up front.

Try it now. A partner wants 30 minutes with Elias tomorrow, but his whole day is trial prep. Say the no out loud, with the reason and an alternative.

frames.title: Setting Realistic Deadlines
frames.text:
A deadline nobody checked against the actual work isn't a deadline; it's a hope. And a hope feels fine right up until it's missed.

First, think about the actual work involved before you name a date. Next, as an EA you often set dates for work someone else is doing, so check with that person before you promise anything on their behalf.

frames.title: Setting Realistic Deadlines
frames.text: Then, add some breathing room for real uncertainty, but don't pad everything by habit.

frames.title: Setting Realistic Deadlines
frames.text:
After that, say the date clearly with a name attached, just like the timeline in an ACT email. Finally, if it starts to slip, say so early, while there are still options.

Here's a situation to work through. Elias promised a client a memo by Monday without asking the associate, who's on leave until Tuesday. It's Friday. What do you do now, and what do you suggest for next time?

frames.title: Time Tracking Done Right
frames.text:
Record your time as you go, because by Friday your memory is guessing.

Try remembering exactly what you did last Tuesday at 2 PM. You can't. That's why time logged at the end of the week comes out vague and short, and the firm loses money it earned.

frames.title: Time Tracking Done Right
frames.text:
First, describe each entry clearly enough that someone else could understand it.

Next, log the small stuff too. Five minutes here and there adds up to real money over a year.

frames.title: Time Tracking Done Right
frames.text:
Then, include calls and emails. They're real work and the most forgotten. Finally, keep a weekly summary, even for unbilled work, so you can see where your time really goes.

Pause the video and rewrite these entries: 'Calls 0.5,' 'Admin 1.2,' 'Harlow stuff 0.8.' Use action, object and purpose, and tag each one to a matter.

frames.title: The Weekly Time Audit
frames.text:
Where you think your time goes and where it actually goes are almost never the same.

Most of us believe we spend our days on the important work. Track a real week, and you'll usually find that work squeezed into the gaps, with reactive meetings taking over. The gap between those two pictures is the useful part.

frames.title: The Weekly Time Audit
frames.text:
First, track one normal week as it really happens.

Next, compare it with what you thought your priorities were.

Then, treat this as an occasional check-up, not something you do forever.

frames.title: The Weekly Time Audit
frames.text:
After that, make sure your time tracking is accurate, because the audit is only as good as the data. Finally, change something next week based on what you found.

Take a second with this one. Your audit shows 40 percent of your week went to rescheduling meetings and only 10 percent to Elias's most important matter. What two things do you change next week, and how would you check it worked?

frames.title: Calendar Management
frames.text: Section 2 of 4: Calendar Management. Eight lessons on keeping a calendar that holds, from conflicts and deep-work blocks to time zones and last-minute changes.

frames.title: Calendar Management That Holds
frames.text:
One calendar everyone trusts, with breathing room built in and a quick weekly check, is what makes a schedule hold.

The moment someone keeps a second, private calendar, conflicts start hiding in the gap between the two. And a calendar that's clean on Monday can be a mess by Friday.

frames.title: Calendar Management That Holds
frames.text:
First, put everything in one synced calendar and retire any side calendars.

Next, leave gaps between commitments by default, and let booking tools handle routine scheduling.

frames.title: Calendar Management That Holds
frames.text: Then, if the firm uses a CRM, make sure scheduling information lives there too, not scattered.

frames.title: Calendar Management That Holds
frames.text:
After that, treat deep-work time as seriously as a meeting. Finally, review the calendar once a week to catch the slow creep of conflicts.

Here's a situation to work through. Elias has a firm calendar, a personal Google calendar, and a paper diary his old assistant used for 'private things.' Last week a client meeting was booked on top of a doctor's appointment. What's your plan to make one calendar everyone trusts?

frames.title: Calendar Conflict & Prioritization Discipline
frames.text:
When two meetings collide, you flag it straight away and recommend, but the executive decides.

It's tempting to just fix it quietly. But Elias might know something the calendar doesn't show: that the 'routine' check-in is a delicate conversation, or that the new client is a big opportunity.

First, tell him as soon as you spot the clash. Don't rebook or decline anything on your own. Next, weigh each meeting by how much it matters, not by which was booked first.

frames.title: Calendar Conflict & Prioritization Discipline
frames.text: Then, lay out the trade-off and say which way you'd go.

frames.title: Calendar Conflict & Prioritization Discipline
frames.text:
After that, write down what was decided, so nobody argues it again later. Finally, let both sides know the outcome quickly.

Try this one. Thursday at 11 a.m., a partner has booked Elias for a budget review, and a major client has just asked for a call at the same time. You could easily move the budget review yourself. What do you do instead, and what does your message to Elias say?

frames.title: Calendar Blocking for Deep Work
frames.text:
A focus block anyone can book over is just a suggestion.

If a calendar only shows meetings, the thinking work, the drafting and the reviewing, has nowhere to live, so it gets squeezed into evenings. A real block is one that can't be taken without a conversation first.

frames.title: Calendar Blocking for Deep Work
frames.text:
First, put real, uninterrupted time on the calendar for focused work.

Next, set it up so it actually can't be booked over.

Then, use it for the most important work, not whatever's easiest to fit.

frames.title: Calendar Blocking for Deep Work
frames.text:
After that, if it does get double-booked, treat that as a real conflict to sort out. Finally, check whether the blocks are being used. One that's always skipped needs fixing or rethinking.

Here's a situation to think about. Elias has a protected block every Tuesday afternoon, but he uses it for email. Meanwhile, the Meridian brief is always done late at night. How do you raise it, and what would you suggest?

frames.title: Buffer Time Between Meetings
frames.text:
Five to ten minutes between meetings is part of the job, not dead space.

Back-to-back, every meeting either starts late or ends in a rush, and people walk into the next one still thinking about the last. A short gap gives time to jot down what just happened and get ready for what's next.

frames.title: Buffer Time Between Meetings
frames.text:
First, make a short gap between meetings your normal setting.

Next, for Elias specifically, remember his standing rule: a debrief buffer after key sessions.

frames.title: Buffer Time Between Meetings
frames.text:
After that, if a day is too packed for gaps, say so instead of silently stacking meetings. Finally, check each week, because back-to-back booking sneaks back in.

Take a second with this one. A new partner books Elias for a call right after a court hearing, not knowing about the debrief rule. What do you say to the partner, and how do you stop it happening again?

frames.title: Recurring Meeting Hygiene
frames.text:
If nobody can say what a meeting is for, it's a good candidate to cut.

Recurring meetings are easy to start, and almost nobody ever ends them. Months later, the reason is gone, but the meeting isn't.

First, every quarter or so, ask of each one: does this still need to happen, this often, with all these people? Next, try the one-sentence test: can anyone say what it's for?

frames.title: Recurring Meeting Hygiene
frames.text: Then, point out meetings that have outlived their purpose, even if nobody else has.

frames.title: Recurring Meeting Hygiene
frames.text:
After that, suggest something specific: cancel it, shorten it or invite fewer people. Finally, check back later that the change stuck.

Think about this one. Elias has a weekly 60-minute 'matter sync' with eight people, no agenda and half of them with cameras off. What would you suggest, and how would you say it to him?

frames.title: Time Zone Management for Distributed Teams
frames.text:
A time that's easy for you might be the middle of the night for someone else.

When people are spread across cities, check everyone's local time, every time. And watch daylight saving, because different countries switch on different dates.

frames.title: Time Zone Management for Distributed Teams
frames.text:
First, check the local time for every person on the invite, not just your own.

Next, name the time zone in the invite itself, so nobody relies on their app to convert it.

frames.title: Time Zone Management for Distributed Teams
frames.text: Then, double-check repeating meetings around the daylight saving changes.

frames.title: Time Zone Management for Distributed Teams
frames.text:
After that, choose a time that's fair to the person worst off, not just convenient for most. Finally, if a mix-up happens, fix it right away and confirm with everyone.

Pause the video and try this. Elias needs a call with co-counsel in London and a client in Manila this week. Find a time that works for all three, and write the line in the invite that names the time zone.

frames.title: Handling Last-Minute Calendar Changes
frames.text:
Before you say yes to a last-minute change, look at what it knocks over.

Moving one meeting is rarely just one meeting. It can push into the next one, cut into prep time or clash with travel.

So first, when a change arrives, don't confirm it yet. Next, see what it pushes out of the way.

frames.title: Handling Last-Minute Calendar Changes
frames.text: Then, work out who else is affected.

frames.title: Handling Last-Minute Calendar Changes
frames.text:
After that, tell everyone involved clearly. Quietly editing the calendar isn't enough, because people plan around what they were told. Finally, recheck the rest of the day, and if the same person keeps causing last-minute changes, deal with that separately.

Here's one to work through. At 10:15, a client asks to move their 2 p.m. meeting to 11:30 today. That slot has Elias's debrief buffer and a call with a junior associate. What do you check before you say yes, and who do you tell?

frames.title: Multi-Calendar Coordination
frames.text:
Check every calendar before you confirm anything, not just the one in front of you.

Many executives live on several calendars: work, personal, board roles. A clash can hide in plain sight because each one looks clear on its own. The master view on the slide is simply the habit of looking across all of them at once.

frames.title: Multi-Calendar Coordination
frames.text:
First, find out every calendar the executive actually uses.

Next, check any new booking against all of them.

frames.title: Multi-Calendar Coordination
frames.text: Then, build a single overall view, even if that means checking each one by hand.

frames.title: Multi-Calendar Coordination
frames.text:
After that, keep work and personal calendars separate for privacy, while you still coordinate across both. Finally, raise a clash across calendars like any other conflict.

Here's a situation to work through. A partner asks you to book Elias for Saturday morning. His firm calendar is empty, but the family calendar shows a school event. What do you do, without sharing private family details with the partner?

frames.title: Legal Calendaring
frames.text: Section 3 of 4: Legal Calendaring. Seven lessons on court deadlines and trial work, including court docketing, counting legal deadlines and e-filing.

frames.title: Court Docketing Workflows
frames.text:
With court deadlines, one missed reminder should never be enough to miss the deadline.

Missing one can cost a client their rights or expose the firm to a malpractice claim. So a good docketing system has backups on purpose.

First, enter each deadline as soon as you know it, straight from the court order or filing confirmation. Next, set reminders at several points, for example two weeks out, three days out and on the day.

frames.title: Court Docketing Workflows
frames.text:
Finally, regularly compare the docket with the case file, and close off deadlines that are done so the open ones stand out.

Here's a situation to think about. An associate emails: 'The judge gave us until the 15th for the reply, please calendar it.' The order itself isn't attached. What do you do before you enter the date?

frames.title: Counting Legal Deadlines: Calendar Days vs. Court Days
frames.text:
A court deadline missed by one day can cost a client their case, so the counting itself is a skill.

In federal court, you count every calendar day, weekends and holidays included. You don't count the day of the event that starts the clock, you do count the last day, and if the last day falls on a weekend or holiday, it moves to the next business day.

Many state courts count 'court days' instead, which skip weekends and court holidays. And how a paper was served can add time; in federal court, service by mail adds three days.

frames.title: Counting Legal Deadlines: Calendar Days vs. Court Days
frames.text:
First, we find the trigger, the event that starts the clock, and note where it came from.

Next, we find the rule that sets the period, and whether it's calendar days or court days, including local rules.

Then we count, and check where the last day lands.

frames.title: Counting Legal Deadlines: Calendar Days vs. Court Days
frames.text:
After that, we enter it in the docketing calendar with the rule cited and reminders at 14, 7 and 2 days. Finally, a second person confirms every calculated court deadline.

Now try a count. A motion is served electronically on Friday, October 2, in federal court, and the response is due in 14 days. When is it due? What changes if the court counts court days instead? And what would you do if the software's date and your hand count don't match?

frames.title: Quick Check
frames.text:
Quick check. You're counting a 10-day response deadline from the day a motion was served. Which day is day 1? Is it the day the motion was served, the day after the motion was served, the first business day of the following week, or whichever day the attorney prefers to use? Take a second.

It's the day after. The day of the event that starts the clock isn't counted, so day 1 is the next day. Then check the court's rules and whether the last day lands on a weekend or court holiday.

frames.title: E-Filing & Service Basics
frames.text:
A brief that's written perfectly but filed wrong is, as far as the court's concerned, not filed.

Two words to keep apart: filing and service. Filing gives the document to the court. Service delivers it to the other side. Federal courts use a system called CM/ECF for e-filing, and PACER to look up records; state courts have their own. The court's confirmation is our proof of filing. Many courts serve registered lawyers automatically, but anyone not registered, like someone without a lawyer, has to be served another way.

frames.title: E-Filing & Service Basics
frames.text:
First, before filing day, we check the rules: PDF format, page limits, file size, exhibit labels, fees and the cut-off time.

Next, we prepare exactly what the attorney approved, redact what the rules require and get final sign-off.

Then we file early, because systems slow down and rejections take time to fix.

frames.title: E-Filing & Service Basics
frames.text:
After that, we save the filed copy and the confirmation together and send the confirmation to the attorney. Finally, we serve anyone outside the system and calendar the new deadlines the filing creates.

Here's a situation to work through. It's 4 p.m. on the deadline day. The court's e-filing system rejects Elias's brief because an exhibit is over the file-size limit. What do you do, in order, and who do you tell?

frames.title: Statute-of-Limitations Rules
frames.text:
Miss the filing deadline for a claim, and the claim can be gone for good, however strong it was.

That outer deadline is the statute of limitations, and it changes with the type of claim and the state or country. A date that was right for last month's case can be completely wrong for this one.

First, work it out and record it when the matter comes in, using the actual date of the event and the right jurisdiction's rule. Next, give it more warning time and reminders than a normal court date.

frames.title: Statute-of-Limitations Rules
frames.text:
Finally, if it's unclear which rule applies, ask the attorney. That's a legal judgment, not ours to make alone.

Here's a situation to think about. A colleague copied the limitation deadline from a similar case last year. The new case is in a different state and involves a government defendant. What's the risk, and who should confirm the real date?

frames.title: Deposition Scheduling
frames.text:
For a deposition, no reply doesn't mean yes.

A deposition is a meeting with far more moving parts: lawyers from both sides, the witness, a court reporter, sometimes an interpreter. Moving it later is expensive, so the work is all in the coordination up front.

First, confirm everyone who has to be there before you lock the date. Next, book the court reporter and any interpreter the moment the date is set. They're usually the hardest to get.

frames.title: Deposition Scheduling
frames.text:
Finally, send the formal notice promptly and keep track of who has actually confirmed.

Take a second with this one. You've confirmed a date with the attorney and the witness, but opposing counsel hasn't answered for days. Do you send the notice or wait? What do you actually do?

frames.title: Exhibits, Binders & Bates Numbering
frames.text:
In a hearing, everyone has to be looking at exactly the same page at the same moment. That's what exhibits and Bates numbers are for.

An exhibit is any document or object used as evidence, like an email, a contract or a photo, and each gets a label, like Exhibit 12 or Exhibit C. Bates numbering stamps a unique number on every page produced in discovery, with a prefix like Thorne 000001, so any page can be found and there's a record of exactly what was handed over.

Binders put the exhibits in order with a tabbed index, usually in several sets: the judge's, the witness's, opposing counsel's and ours.

frames.title: Exhibits, Binders & Bates Numbering
frames.text:
First, we follow the court's and judge's rules for labels.

Next, we keep a master exhibit list: number, description, date, Bates range and status.

Then we apply Bates numbers with software, never by hand, and never renumber a set that's been produced.

frames.title: Exhibits, Binders & Bates Numbering
frames.text:
After that, we build every binder from the master list. Finally, we check every set page by page and keep a digital copy of each.

Here's a situation to work through. Two days before a hearing, Elias adds three exhibits between Exhibits 7 and 8. Four binder sets are already printed. How do you handle the numbering and the binders, and what do you tell opposing counsel?

frames.title: War Room Trial Support
frames.text:
A trial isn't a busy week; it's a completely different way of working, so agree the rules before it starts.

The attorney's day is squeezed and everything is urgent, so you're properly on call.

First, before trial starts, ask exactly what support the attorney will need: documents, research, exhibits. Next, organize every document, contact and practical detail, like the courthouse address and parking, so you can find it instantly.

frames.title: War Room Trial Support
frames.text:
Finally, agree how you'll communicate during trial: which channel, and how fast you'll respond.

Take a second with this one. On day two of a trial, Elias texts at 7 a.m. asking for an exhibit that isn't in the trial binder. What should have been done before trial, and what do you do now?

frames.title: Travel Management
frames.text: Section 4 of 4: Travel Management. Eleven lessons on planning travel end-to-end, from itineraries and visas to contingency plans and the post-trip debrief.

frames.title: Executive Travel Logistics — Domestic & International Itineraries
frames.text:
Plan the trip backward, starting from what has to go right when the executive arrives.

Most people plan forward: flight, then hotel, then 'we'll sort out the car.' Planning backward starts with the meeting or hearing at the other end, and makes sure every piece before it supports it.

frames.title: Executive Travel Logistics — Domestic & International Itineraries
frames.text:
First, ask what Elias must be ready for, and when. Then work back through the car, the hotel and the flights.

Next, for international trips, check the visa and document rules well ahead of time.

frames.title: Executive Travel Logistics — Domestic & International Itineraries
frames.text:
Finally, leave real room between connecting flights, especially when he lands internationally and has to clear customs again.

Here's a situation to think about. Elias's inbox has seven separate confirmation emails for one trip: two flights, a hotel, two car transfers, a restaurant and a train. He asks, 'What time is my car tomorrow?' What should you have sent him instead?

frames.title: Visa & Documentation Requirements
frames.text:
Check the entry rules for this trip today; don't rely on what was true last time.

Entry requirements change, and every country is different. A trip can be ruined at the airport by a passport that's valid but not valid enough, or a visa that takes weeks longer than expected.

frames.title: Visa & Documentation Requirements
frames.text: First, check how long the passport is still valid. Many countries want six months left after the trip ends.

frames.title: Visa & Documentation Requirements
frames.text: Then, start any visa early.

frames.title: Visa & Documentation Requirements
frames.text:
After that, sort supporting papers like invitation letters early enough to fix problems. Finally, write down what was needed, so the next trip starts with facts.

Pause the video and work through this. Elias flies to Singapore for a deposition in five weeks, and his passport expires in four months. What do you check, what do you do today and what do you tell him?

frames.title: International Travel Considerations
frames.text:
Going abroad means planning for health, money and local customs, not just flights and hotels.

None of it is hard, but all of it needs doing before he leaves.

frames.title: International Travel Considerations
frames.text:
First, check health and safety for the destination: vaccinations, safety advisories and local emergency numbers.

Next, sort out how he'll pay. Will his card work there, and does he need cash?

Then, learn the local business customs, how meetings run and how people greet each other, so he doesn't get caught out.

frames.title: International Travel Considerations
frames.text:
After that, look at the government travel advisory again close to departure. Finally, give international trips more planning time than domestic ones.

Here's a situation to work through. You booked Elias's trip three weeks ago. Two days before he leaves, the government issues an advisory about protests near his hotel. What do you do?

frames.title: Managing Multi-City, Multi-Leg Itineraries
frames.text:
In a trip with several stops, look for the tightest connection, because that's where it will break.

With one flight there and back, a delay is annoying. With four legs, a delay on the first can knock over every connection after it.

So first, lay out every leg together, not one at a time. Next, find the tightest connection and give it extra time.

frames.title: Managing Multi-City, Multi-Leg Itineraries
frames.text: Then, make sure each car pickup and hotel check-in matches the real arrival times.

frames.title: Managing Multi-City, Multi-Leg Itineraries
frames.text:
After that, put the whole trip on one page. Finally, check it all again just before departure, in case any times have shifted.

Pause the video and look at this trip: New York to Atlanta with a 50-minute connection, on to Dallas for two days of trial prep, then Dallas to Phoenix for a mediation. Where's the weak point, and what would you change?

frames.title: Ground Transportation Coordination
frames.text:
'We'll figure out a car when we land' is how good trips go wrong.

The car gets treated as an afterthought, until the executive is standing at the curb at night with no ride. Plan the ride as carefully as the flight.

First, confirm the exact pickup time, the exact spot and a phone number for the driver.

frames.title: Ground Transportation Coordination
frames.text: Then, check who's traveling: children need car seats, and some people need accessible vehicles.

frames.title: Ground Transportation Coordination
frames.text:
After that, for important trips, have a backup ride ready. Finally, reconfirm the booking a day or so before travel.

Pause the video and try this. Elias and his two young children land in Orlando at 9:40 PM. Write the ride confirmation you'd send him, with every detail it needs.

frames.title: Loyalty Programs & Travel Preferences
frames.text:
Adding the loyalty number to every booking is a small habit that pays off on every single trip.

Those numbers bring upgrades, priority service and status, and the benefits grow the more they're used. Leaving one off is money and comfort left on the table.

frames.title: Loyalty Programs & Travel Preferences
frames.text:
First, keep all the membership numbers with Elias's other preferences.

Next, add them to every booking as a normal step.

frames.title: Loyalty Programs & Travel Preferences
frames.text: Then, apply his seat, route and hotel preferences at the same time.

frames.title: Loyalty Programs & Travel Preferences
frames.text:
After that, put it on a checklist, so you don't rely on memory when you're rushing. Finally, check the details now and then, because status levels change.

Here's a situation to think about. A substitute assistant books Elias a middle seat with a connecting flight, not knowing his preferences. What in your process would have prevented this, even with someone new doing the booking?

frames.title: Travel Risk Contingency Planning
frames.text:
The backup plan should exist before the trip, not be invented in the middle of a crisis.

When a flight is cancelled, the worst place to be is starting your research from scratch while the executive waits at the gate. The assistant who planned ahead is already making the call while everyone else is still searching.

First, before you finalize the trip, list the realistic things that could go wrong. Next, find the backup for each in advance: the next flight, another route, a local contact.

frames.title: Travel Risk Contingency Planning
frames.text: Then, keep those backups with the itinerary, where you can find them fast.

frames.title: Travel Risk Contingency Planning
frames.text:
After that, if something happens, use the backup straight away. It's the same idea as having a backup vendor: it's ready before you need it.

Pause the video and work this one out. Elias flies Chicago to Denver, then on to Boise for a 10 AM hearing. What are the two most likely problems, and what's the backup for each?

frames.title: Emergency Flight Contingencies
frames.text:
Know the one time the trip absolutely has to hit, and the backup, before the plane leaves.

On a court appearance or a closing, a cancelled flight can wreck the whole reason for going. So you plan around that fixed point.

First, identify the deadline the travel must meet, like the hearing time, before you book. Next, know the backups ahead of time: a later flight, a different airport or a car for the last stretch.

frames.title: Emergency Flight Contingencies
frames.text:
Finally, when something goes wrong, send the executive one clear message with the problem and your plan, not a stream of updates.

Take a second with this one. A storm grounds flights out of Chicago. Elias is stuck overnight, and his 9 a.m. client meeting in New York is at risk. What options do you prepare, and what do you tell the client, and when?

frames.title: Expense Tracking While Traveling
frames.text:
Snap the receipt the moment you get it, and note the client while you still remember.

On the road, receipts end up in pockets, cars and hotel bins, and rebuilding a trip's expenses a week later from memory is slow and usually wrong.

First, capture each receipt immediately, even just a photo. Next, note which client or matter it belongs to.

frames.title: Expense Tracking While Traveling
frames.text: Then, handle it the same way as normal expenses, just faster.

frames.title: Expense Tracking While Traveling
frames.text:
After that, spend two minutes each evening checking nothing from the day is missing. Finally, submit everything within a set time after getting back.

Here's a situation to work through. Elias returns from a four-day trip with a crumpled pile of receipts: two client dinners, three taxis, a hotel, a personal gift and a coffee with no note. How do you sort them, and what do you do differently next trip?

frames.title: Building a Real Travel Checklist
frames.text:
A checklist that lives only in your head isn't really a checklist.

Every time you rely on memory, you forget something different. Write it down once, use it every trip and improve it a little each time, just like the Home Binder.

frames.title: Building a Real Travel Checklist
frames.text:
First, give passport and visa their own section, so they never get lost among the bookings.

Next, add health and safety prep for the destination.

frames.title: Building a Real Travel Checklist
frames.text:
Then, include a check that loyalty numbers were added, and a contact for emergencies. Finally, keep it somewhere you'll find it.

Pause the video and try this. Elias's last trip had three small misses: no power adapter, a missing loyalty number and no emergency contact for the hotel. Turn those into checklist items, and say which section each belongs in.

frames.title: Post-Trip Debrief & Follow-Up
frames.text:
The trip isn't over when the traveler gets home; the last steps make the next trip better.

Three things usually get skipped: the expenses, the thank-yous and writing down what went wrong. That last one matters most, or the same problem happens again next time.

First, reconcile the expenses soon after return. Next, send any thank-you notes or follow-ups while they still mean something.

frames.title: Post-Trip Debrief & Follow-Up
frames.text: Then, write a short note on what worked and what didn't while it's fresh.

frames.title: Post-Trip Debrief & Follow-Up
frames.text:
After that, feed that note into the travel preferences or checklist. It's the same improvement habit you'll use for bigger projects on Day 6.

Pause the video and try this. Elias's Denver hotel had no quiet place to work, and his return connection was too tight. Write the debrief note, and say where each lesson gets recorded.

frames.title: Practice Lab
frames.text: Time to practice what you just learned. In the Calendar Conflict Resolver and Travel Planning lab, you'll take a full attorney's week of overlapping commitments, resolve it and turn it into a BLUF briefing. Then you'll plan the attorney's business trip to a Chicago arbitration end-to-end: flights, hotel, ground transport and stops. It's your turn now.
